shortDescription: From Babylonia to Roman Africa and China, the followers of the prophet Mani held that Light and Darkness were mixed in the world. Their Elect lived in strict purity and poverty, and their Hearers fed and served them.

timeline.headline: Mani is born in Babylonia and receives his first revelation

lines.when: 216, the year 527 of the era of the Babylonian astronomers
lines.text: Mani is born in a village called Mardinu, on the upper canal of Kutha, in the fourth year of King Adharban. Biruni gives the place and date from Mani's own book.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29094-29098; the year is a conversion of the era Biruni names, the era of Alexander

lines.text: The Fihrist, a Baghdad scholar's book of the 900s, says Mani's father joined people of the district of Dastumeisan known as the Mughtasila, those who wash themselves. Remnants of them, it says, still lived there and in the marsh country.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, in Flügel's German, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 4366-4371

lines.when: in his thirteenth year, the second year of Ardashir, King of Kings
lines.text: Biruni writes that Mani received his first revelation in his thirteenth year.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29098-29100

lines.when: when he had completed his twelfth year
lines.text: By Mani's own account, as the Fihrist gives it, an angel called at-Taum, a word it glosses as companion, told him to leave that community: he did not belong among them, and his task was purity and the taming of desire.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 4390-4399
lines.note: The Fihrist and Biruni give his age a year apart.

lines.when: when he had completed his twenty-fourth year
lines.text: The angel came again, the Fihrist says, and told him the time had come to come out in public and preach his teaching aloud.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 4400-4404

timeline.headline: Mani writes his own scriptures and lays down laws for the Elect and the Hearers

lines.text: Mani writes a book for King Shapur, son of Ardashir. It begins, Biruni says, with God's messengers bringing wisdom and deeds from age to age: the Buddha to India, Zoroaster to Persia, Jesus to the West, and in this last age Mani himself to Babylonia.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29054-29061

lines.text: Biruni writes that Mani called himself the Paraclete, the Helper the Messiah had announced, and the seal of the prophets, the last of them.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29061-29064

lines.text: Mani writes many books, Biruni says, among them his gospel, the book for Shapur, the Treasure of Life and the Book of the Giants. The Fihrist counts seven, one in Persian and six in Syriac.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29111-29115; Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 5243-5244

lines.text: Mani teaches that light and darkness are without beginning and end, Biruni writes, and forbids his followers to slaughter or hurt animals, or to hurt fire, water and plants.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29069-29071

lines.text: For the Elect, the saints and ascetics, his laws allow no property but food for one day and clothing for one year, forbid them sexual intercourse, and send them wandering through the world to preach.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29072-29079

lines.text: For the Hearers, the lay followers, his laws ask a tenth of their property as alms, fasting for a seventh part of their life, one wife, and care for the Elect.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29081-29085

lines.text: The Fihrist gives the rule of four or seven prayers a day, said standing, after washing, turned toward the great light, then bowing down.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 4936-4940

lines.when: on the day Shapur was crowned
lines.text: The Fihrist, from what the Manichaeans said, has Mani first come forward in public on the day Shapur took the crown. Later, it says, Shapur honored him and granted that his followers go freely through his realm.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 4415-4420, 4449-4462
lines.note: The sources differ: one of Biruni's informants told him Shapur banished Mani (lines 29161-29171).

timeline.headline: Mani dies at the hands of a Persian king, and his followers flee east

lines.when: when Bahram, son of Hurmuz, came to the throne
lines.text: Biruni writes that the faith grew under Ardashir, Shapur and Hurmuz, until King Bahram came to the throne. Bahram had Mani sought out, saying: "This man has come forward calling people to destroy the world."
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29117-29122

lines.text: It is well known, Biruni writes, that the king had Mani flayed, his skin filled with grass and hung at the gate of Gundeshapur, still called the Mani-gate.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29125-29127

lines.text: A book by one of Mani's pupils, as Biruni reports it, says Mani failed to cure a relative of the king and was chained hand and foot in prison until he died.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29130-29138
lines.note: The accounts of his death differ.

lines.text: The Fihrist says Mani was killed and hung in two halves at two gates of Gundeshapur, and that others say he died in prison.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 5112-5127

lines.text: Alexander of Lycopolis heard that Mani lived when Valerian was emperor, served under Shapur, king of the Persians, and was put to death after offending him in some way.
lines.reference: Alexander of Lycopolis, Of the Manichaeans 2, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 24496-24498

lines.text: The Fihrist says the king forbade religious disputes and killed Mani's followers wherever he found them, until they crossed the river of Balkh into the lands of the Khan, the title of the Turks' rulers.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 5388-5396

lines.text: His followers keep the day Mani was killed as their great feast, the Bema, with a platform of five steps covered in precious cloth. Augustine says they kept Easter with little care, and told him the day to keep was the death of one who truly suffered.
lines.reference: Augustine, Against the Letter of Mani called Fundamental 8, Latin, cic/texts/augustine_arian-sermon-collatio-maximinum-pl42-lat_migne1886.txt lines 12877-12902; English, cic/texts/npnf104_augustine-anti-manichaean-anti-donatist.xml lines 3733-3735
lines.note: Augustine kept the feast as a Hearer.

timeline.when: From about 300, in the Roman world
timeline.headline: Their teachers reach Egypt, and church writers answer them

lines.text: Alexander of Lycopolis, in Egypt, writes that he learned Mani's teaching from one Papus, then from Thomas, and others after them.
lines.reference: Alexander of Lycopolis, Of the Manichaeans 2, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 24494-24496

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Mani called himself the Paraclete, chose twelve disciples, and brought his teaching from Persia to the Roman world, where the name of the Manichaeans is still common.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.31, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42484-42497
lines.note: An enemy, writing in the early 300s.

lines.text: Cyril of Jerusalem names the meetings of the Marcionists and Manichees among the heretics' gatherings that are also called churches.
lines.reference: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 18.26, cic/texts/npnf207_cyril-jerusalem-gregory-nazianzen.xml lines 20352-20357

lines.text: Ephrem argues against Mani, who, he says, calls God the Earth of Light, bounded on one side by the Darkness.
lines.reference: Ephrem, Prose Refutations, cic/texts/ephraim_prose-refutations_mitchell1912-1921.txt line 640

timeline.when: 372 to 399, in the Roman Empire and Roman Africa
timeline.headline: Roman laws strike at their meetings, and Augustine, once a Hearer, answers them

lines.when: 372, in the consulship of Modestus and Arinthaeus
lines.text: The emperors Valentinian and Valens order that wherever the Manichaeans meet, their teachers be heavily fined, the members cut off from society, and the houses where the profane teaching is taught seized.
lines.reference: Theodosian Code XVI.5.3, cic/texts/theodosianus-16_mommsen-meyer1905.txt lines 86093-86097; the year from the consuls the law names

lines.when: from his nineteenth year to his twenty-eighth
lines.text: Augustine is a Hearer for nine years. He carries food to the Elect, out of which, he writes in mockery, their stomachs were to make angels and gods to set the Hearers free.
lines.reference: Augustine, Confessions IV.1, cic/texts/npnf101_augustine-confessions-letters.xml lines 6334-6346; Latin, cic/texts/augustine_confessiones-lat_knoll-csel33.txt lines 5683-5684, 5730-5733; a Hearer, Debate with Fortunatus 2, cic/texts/augustine_arian-sermon-collatio-maximinum-pl42-lat_migne1886.txt lines 7684-7685
lines.note: Augustine's mockery, written after he left them.

lines.text: Faustus, a bishop of the Manichaeans, comes to Carthage.
lines.reference: Augustine, Confessions V.3, cic/texts/npnf101_augustine-confessions-letters.xml lines 7632-7635; Latin, cic/texts/augustine_confessiones-lat_knoll-csel33.txt lines 7334-7336

lines.when: 28 August 392, in the second consulship of Arcadius, with Rufinus
lines.text: At Hippo, in the Baths of Sossius, before the people, Augustine debates Fortunatus, a Manichaean priest. Fortunatus calls on him as witness to their way of life.
lines.reference: Augustine, Debate with Fortunatus 1, Latin, cic/texts/augustine_arian-sermon-collatio-maximinum-pl42-lat_migne1886.txt lines 7609-7611, 7658-7667

lines.text: Augustine answers that he was a Hearer, not one of the Elect. At their prayer he saw nothing shameful, only that they prayed facing the sun, against the faith he later learned.
lines.reference: Augustine, Debate with Fortunatus 1-2, Latin, cic/texts/augustine_arian-sermon-collatio-maximinum-pl42-lat_migne1886.txt lines 7683-7692, 7710-7711

lines.text: Faustus writes a book of short answers to the questions their opponents raise. Augustine sets out each of its parts as Faustus wrote it before he answers.
lines.reference: Augustine, Reply to Faustus I.1-2, cic/texts/npnf104_augustine-anti-manichaean-anti-donatist.xml lines 4312-4315

lines.text: Christians bring Faustus and some others before the proconsul. Found to be a Manichaean, Faustus is only exiled to an island, because those same Christians plead for him, and not long after all are released together.
lines.reference: Augustine, Reply to Faustus V.8, cic/texts/npnf104_augustine-anti-manichaean-anti-donatist.xml lines 4615-4616; Latin, cic/texts/augustine_arian-sermon-collatio-maximinum-pl42-lat_migne1886.txt lines 16830-16840
lines.note: Augustine calls the exile the lightest of penalties.

lines.text: A law to the emperors' deputy for Africa orders that the Manichaeans be sought out, brought into public and punished most severely, with those who shelter them in their houses.
lines.reference: Theodosian Code XVI.5.35, cic/texts/theodosianus-16_mommsen-meyer1905.txt lines 87272-87278; the year from the consul the law names

timeline.headline: Bishop Leo finds many of them hidden in the city

lines.when: 443, in the second consulship of Maximus, with Paterius
lines.text: Prosper writes that Leo, bishop of Rome, learned that many Manichaeans lay hidden in the city. He had them brought out before the whole church, made them condemn and disclose their teaching, and burned their books.
lines.reference: Prosper of Aquitaine, Chronicle, cic/texts/prosper_chronica-minora-1-lat_mommsen1892.txt lines 54712-54717

timeline.when: 732 to 843, among the Uyghurs and in China
timeline.headline: Uyghur rulers favor the faith, and China first limits it, then closes its temples

lines.text: A Chinese emperor's order calls Mani's teaching a perverse belief that falsely takes the name of Buddhism and deceives the people, and forbids it. The western foreigners, whose own religion it is, may still keep it themselves.
lines.reference: The Tong tien, in Chavannes and Pelliot's French, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 6877-6886; the year is the editors' conversion of the Chinese reign year
lines.note: From a Chinese compilation made between 766 and 801.

lines.text: A stone inscription of the Uyghurs, a Turkish people, says their khagan brought four Manichaean religious into his kingdom, and that their master could initiate the Uyghurs into the true religion.
lines.reference: The Karabalgasun inscription, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 8671-8673, 8750-8751

lines.text: An imperial decree orders that the Uyghurs who keep the Manichaean faith found temples.
lines.reference: Fo tsou t'ong ki, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 12205-12208; the year is the editors' conversion

lines.text: The Uyghurs ask to set up such temples in the prefectural cities of King, Yang, Hong and Yue.
lines.reference: Fo tsou t'ong ki, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 12230-12233; the year is the editors' conversion

lines.text: The Uyghurs come to China bringing tribute, with Manichaeans for the first time, and a temple is set up to lodge them. Their religion, the chronicle says, has them eat only in the evening and take no milk or butter.
lines.reference: Tseu tche t'ong kien, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 12381-12387; the year is the editors' conversion

lines.text: An emperor's letter says the faith was forbidden in China before the t'ien-pao years, and was let grow only because the Uyghurs held it in respect and faith.
lines.reference: Imperial letter, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 13695-13700

lines.text: With the Uyghurs defeated, an edict closes the Manichaean temples across the empire. A Chinese chronicle compiled four centuries later says some seventy of their women religious at the capital all died.
lines.reference: Fo tsou t'ong ki, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_traite-manicheen-retrouve-en-chine-pt2-in-journal-asiatique-11-1-fra_chavannes-pelliot1913.txt lines 14089-14095; the Uyghurs' defeat, the court's order, line 13960; the year is the editors' conversion
lines.note: Another chapter of the same chronicle gives seventy-two (line 14114).

timeline.headline: The Fihrist and Biruni find them few in Islamic lands, and many among the eastern Turks

lines.text: The Fihrist says they fled again to Khorasan, and some five hundred gathered at Samarkand. When the ruler of Khorasan meant to kill them, the ruler of China, as the Fihrist calls him, swore to kill the Muslims in his own lands if one of them was killed, and they were left alone and taxed.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 5406-5427

lines.text: Ibn al-Nadim writes that he had known about three hundred of them in Baghdad, and that barely five were left there in his own time.
lines.reference: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, cic/texts/mani_mani-seine-lehre-und-seine-schriften-fihrist-deu-ara_fluegel1862.txt lines 5427-5431

lines.text: Biruni writes that Mani's followers are scattered in the Muslim lands, with a community at Samarkand, and that most of the eastern Turks, of the people of China and Tibet, and some of the Hindus still hold his law.
lines.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations, cic/texts/biruni_chronology-of-ancient-nations_sachau1879.txt lines 29140-29147

timeline.headline: The Hearers' confession is found near Dunhuang

lines.text: A scroll in Mani's script, in an old Turkish tongue, 14 feet 8 inches long, is among the manuscripts of a cave library near the Dunhuang oasis, part of which M. A. Stein acquires. It lay mixed with Chinese rolls of mostly Buddhist texts.
lines.reference: A. von Le Coq, introduction to the Khuastuanift, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_dr-steins-turkish-khuastuanift-in-jras-1911_le-coq1911.txt lines 15395-15417, 15429-15433
lines.note: The library was found by a Chinese priest. The copy itself is undated.

lines.text: The scroll is the Hearers' confession, a prayer for forgiveness. It says that, because they lived in love of the Demon, the light of the Five-God they took in each day with their food goes to the Bad Place. Each article ends: my God, cleansing ourselves of sin, we pray, forgive my sin.
lines.reference: The Khuastuanift, tr. Le Coq, cic/texts/manichaean-texts_dr-steins-turkish-khuastuanift-in-jras-1911_le-coq1911.txt lines 15727-15729, 17364-17371, 17443-17449

uncertain: Who ruled Babylonia when Mani was born. Biruni dates the birth, from Mani's own book, to the fourth year of King Adharban, whom he believes to be Ardawan, the last of the Ashkanians, the kings who held Iraq before Ardashir rose; by Mani's thirteenth year Ardashir was King of Kings.
Mani's age at his first revelation. The Fihrist says it came when he had completed his twelfth year; Biruni, from Mani's own book, says in his thirteenth year.

How King Shapur received him. The Fihrist, from what the Manichaeans said, has Mani first come forward in public on the day Shapur was crowned, and later has Shapur honor him and grant that his disciples be respected and go freely through his realm, and the Manichaeans add that Mani came in with two lamps of light shining on his shoulders. One of Biruni's informants, the Ispahbadh Marzuban, told him that Shapur banished Mani under Zoroaster's law, which orders false prophets expelled, and that Mani went to India, China and Tibet, came back, and was killed by Bahram for breaking that condition.

Whether Mani worked wonders. Biruni says his followers held two opinions: one party that he worked no miracle, the other that he did, and that King Shapur came to believe in him after Mani rose with him into the air between heaven and earth.

Which king killed Mani, and how. Biruni names Bahram, and says it is well known that he had Mani flayed, his skin filled with grass and hung at the gate of Gundeshapur; a book by one of Mani's pupils, which Biruni reports, has him chained in prison until he died. The Fihrist says he was killed under Bahram and hung in two halves at two gates of the city, and that others say he died in prison. Alexander of Lycopolis, writing in Egypt about 300, heard that he served under Shapur and was put to death after offending him in some way. The Acts of Archelaus, a staged debate of the 300s, also has the king flay him.

Augustine's charges against the Elect. In On the Morals of the Manichaeans he says that in nine years he could not hear of one of their Elect who was not found breaking their rules, or at least suspected of it, and that many were caught at wine and meat, though this, he says, he heard only by report. In the Confessions he mocks their belief that a fig wept when it was plucked, and that the particles of God in it stayed bound unless an Elect set them free with his teeth and belly. These are an opponent's charge and mockery.
The deaths of 843. The Chinese chronicle that reports them, compiled in the 1200s, gives seventy women religious at the capital in one chapter and seventy-two in another, and gives no cause.

quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from the Latin, which the scan breaks across two lines (ora- tioni). Newman's English (lines 3230-3232) leaves the two words out. The Latin has no word for our; it is carried by Fortunatus's words before it, our way of life (nostram conversationem).

quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Le Coq's English; the Old Turkish in the held scan is partly garbled. The sentence begins at lines 17364-17371, with the light of the Five-God that every day we have absorbed in our food.

quotationOriginals.printed: they should make for us angels and gods, by whom we might be delivered
quotationOriginals.work: Augustine, Confessions IV.1, tr. J. G. Pilkington (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, 1)

quotationOriginals.modern: This man has come forward calling people to destroy the world.
quotationOriginals.printed: This man has come forward calling people to destroy the world.
quotationOriginals.work: al-Biruni, The Chronology of Ancient Nations, the account of Mani, tr. C. Edward Sachau (1879)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: King Bahram's words as Biruni gives them, in Sachau's English; the Arabic is not held.

quotationOriginals.modern: If you press me whether I accept the gospel, I may answer: I have left all that was mine. Father, mother, wife, children, gold, silver, eating, drinking, comforts, pleasures. Take this as answer enough to your questions. And believe that you will be blessed, if you do not stumble because of me.
quotationOriginals.printed: I might very well reply to your question whether I believe the gospel, by saying, I have left all, father, mother, wife, children, gold, silver, eating, drinking, luxuries, pleasures; take this as a sufficient answer to your questions, and believe that you will be blessed if you are not offended in me.
quotationOriginals.work: Faustus, in Augustine, Reply to Faustus the Manichaean V.1, tr. Richard Stothert (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, 4); Latin in Migne, Patrologia Latina 42
quotationOriginals.original: si perroganti utrum accipiam Evan- gelium dixero, Omnia mea dimisi, patrem, matrem, - uxorem, filios, aurum, argentum, manducare, bi- A. bere, delicias, voluptates; hoc tibi ad interrogata satis responsum puta, et beatum te futurum, si in me non fueris scandalizatus.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from the Latin, not Stothert's English, which agrees with it clause for clause. The Latin scan breaks Evangelium and bibere across lines, sets a dash before uxorem and a stray letter A between bi- and bere; none of these is part of the text.

quotationOriginals.modern: Every day, how many evil thoughts we think! How many wretched words we speak that should not be spoken! How many deeds we do that should not be done!
quotationOriginals.printed: Every da>-, how many evil thoughts do we think ! how many miserable words, that ought not to be spoken, do we speak ! how many deeds, that ought not to be done, do we do !
quotationOriginals.work: The Khuastuanift, the Hearers' confession, article 15, tr. A. von Le Coq (Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1911)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Le Coq's English; the scan reads da>- for day, and the Old Turkish in it is partly garbled. Le Coq's miserable is given as wretched, since miserable now means unhappy.
